# Lagos Foods Ltd — Employee Handbook (Excerpt)

## Working hours
Standard working hours are 08:30 to 17:00, Monday to Friday. Staff are entitled
to a one-hour lunch break. Remote work is permitted up to two days per week with
line-manager approval.

## Leave policy
- Annual leave: 21 working days per year, accruing monthly.
- Sick leave: up to 10 paid days per year; a medical note is required after two
  consecutive days.
- Maternity leave: 16 weeks fully paid. Paternity leave: 2 weeks fully paid.
- Leave requests must be submitted at least 5 working days in advance through
  the operations manager.

h
  the operations manager.

## Expense reimbursement
Employees may claim approved business expenses. Receipts must be submitted within
30 days. Claims above ₦50,000 require director approval. Reimbursements are paid
with the next payroll run. Personal travel and entertainment are not reimbursable.

## Refund and returns policy (customer-facing)
Customers may return unopened products within 14 days of purchase for a full
refund. Perishable goods are non-refundable once delivered unless they arrive
damaged, in which case a replacement or full refund is issued within 48 hours of
a reported complaint. Refunds are processed to the original payment method within
5 business days.

## Code of conduct
All staff must protect customer data, avoid conflicts of interest, and report
any suspected fraud to the compliance officer immediately.

# Lagos Foods Ltd — 2026 Growth Strategy (Internal)

## Targets
The board has set a Q2 2026 revenue target of ₦52,000,000, representing roughly
15% growth over Q1. Gross margin should be held at or above 38%.

## Priorities
1. Expand the cold-chain delivery network to Ibadan and Abeokuta.
2. Launch the SME wholesale tier with 30-day credit terms for vetted buyers.
3. Reduce customer acquisition cost from ₦1,800 to ₦1,400 by shifting spend to
   referral programmes.

## Risks
- Diesel price volatility affecting logistics cost.
- Currency fluctuation on imported packaging.
- Concentration risk: the top three customers account for 28% of revenue.

Concentration risk: the top three customers account for 28% of revenue.

## Key metrics watched monthly
Revenue, gross margin, on-time delivery rate (target 95%), refund rate (target
below 2%), and repeat-purchase rate (target above 40%).

1. Executive Summary
Aura Identity is a privacy-first, stateless enterprise biometric intelligence platform purpose-built for the Innovation Lab. It delivers two modalities of biometric verification — Face and Voice — through a unified API, without ever storing a single biometric template. Clients own every embedding, every record, and every audit trail.

embedding, every record, and every audit trail.
The platform eliminates the single largest risk in traditional biometric deployments: centralised template databases that become high-value targets for attackers. Instead, Aura acts as a processing engine: it receives raw media, performs inference using pretrained ONNX models, returns a result, and discards the input. Zero retention by design.
Privacy by Architecture
Aura processes biometric data. It does not own it. No face image, voice clip, embedding, or identity record is persisted on the platform side. Full data sovereignty remains with the deploying organisation.

2.2 Use Cases — Face
2.2.1 Customer Onboarding (KYC)
Financial services, telecoms, and fintech platforms use Aura to verify identity during account opening. A customer captures a selfie; Aura checks image quality, runs passive liveness, generates an embedding, and the platform compares it against a government-ID face extracted by the client. The platform returns a match decision with confidence score. No biometric data is stored by Aura.
2.2.2 Continuous Authentication

thentication
Aura embeds into mobile and desktop applications to re-verify the authenticated user at low-friction intervals. Periodic selfie captures are compared against the enrolled embedding stored by the client. Active liveness challenges are triggered on suspicious events.
2.2.3 Physical Access Control
Enterprise facilities use face verification at gates and turnstiles. A camera captures the approaching person; Aura performs 1:many search across enrolled staff embeddings and returns an access decision within sub-200 ms on commodity hardware.
2.2.4 Fraud Prevention

mmerce and financial platforms integrate the risk engine to score high-value transactions. Low liveness scores, deepfake signals, or repeat failed attempts trigger step-up authentication or block actions automatically.
2.2.5 Duplicate Enrolment Detection
During user registration, a new face embedding is compared against all existing embeddings at a high threshold (0.85+). A match indicates the identity has already been enrolled, preventing duplicate or synthetic account creation.
2.3 Use Cases — Voice
2.3.1 Phone Banking & IVR

ather than PIN or memorable information. The caller speaks a passphrase; Aura extracts a speaker embedding, compares it against the stored voiceprint, and returns a verification decision before the agent takes the call.
2.3.2 Voice-Gated Devices & Smart Assistants
IoT devices and smart assistants use Aura to ensure only authorised users can issue sensitive commands. A wake-word triggers a short speaker verification check before processing the instruction.
2.3.3 Passive Voice Authentication in Calls

res the active speaker against the enrolled voiceprint. A significant drop in score raises a flag for agent review without interrupting the customer.
2.3.4 Synthetic Speech & Replay Attack Detection
Anti-spoofing models detect text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis, voice conversion attacks, and recorded replay attacks before verification occurs, preventing presentation attacks through the voice channel.

he platform never becomes a custodian of biometric data. Every inference session is independent. There is no session state, no embedding cache, and no image buffer between requests.

3.5.1 API Key Tiers
Three key tiers enforce least-privilege access. The master key (set at deployment time) provisions other keys. Project keys are scoped to a single service. Organisation keys span a company or tenant. All keys are validated on every request. Revocation is immediate.

4. Face Verification Module
4.1 Overview

cation Module implements end-to-end biometric recognition using the InsightFace model family. It covers the full pipeline from raw image ingestion through face detection, alignment, embedding extraction, comparison, and quality gating.
4.2 Face Detection — SCRFD
Face detection uses SCRFD-10G (det_10g.onnx), a highly efficient single-stage detector based on Sample- and Computation-Redistribution. It processes a 640×640 input across three strides (8, 16, 32) with two anchors per stride. The output includes bounding boxes, per-face confidence scores, and five facial keypoints (two eyes, nose tip, two mouth corners) for each detected face.
4.2.1 Inference Pipeline

(two eyes, nose tip, two mouth corners) for each detected face.
4.2.1 Inference Pipeline
Resize input image to 640×640 while tracking scale factors (sx, sy)
Normalise: (pixel − 127.5) / 128.0, convert to NCHW float32
Run SCRFD inference → decode bounding boxes and keypoints with stride-adjusted centres
Apply Non-Maximum Suppression (IoU threshold 0.45)
Sort detections by confidence score descending
Return top face (highest score) for embedding pipeline; all faces for /image/detect
4.3 Face Alignment

nonical 112×112 template using a partial affine transform estimated from the five detected keypoints. This alignment step is critical: it normalises pose, scale, and in-plane rotation, giving the recognition model a consistent input regardless of how the face was positioned in the original image.
The canonical keypoint template positions are:
Left eye:   [38.29, 51.70]     Right eye:  [73.53, 51.50]
Nose tip:   [56.03, 71.74]
Left mouth: [41.55, 92.37]     Right mouth:[70.73, 92.20]
4.4 Face Recognition — ArcFace

ebFace600K dataset (w600k_r50.onnx). ArcFace optimises an additive angular margin loss that pushes inter-class angles to be large and intra-class angles small, producing highly discriminative 512-dimensional embeddings. The output vector is L2-normalised so that cosine similarity equals the dot product between two unit vectors.

4.5 Liveness Detection
4.5.1 Passive Liveness
Passive liveness analysis runs on a single image without requiring any user action. It uses four complementary signals:

ssive liveness analysis runs on a single image without requiring any user action. It uses four complementary signals:
These signals are combined into a liveness score (0–1). Scores ≥ 0.60 are classified as real, ≤ 0.35 as spoof, and the middle range as uncertain. Spoof type is inferred: low HF ratio combined with flat saturation indicates a printed photo; high bright ratio indicates a screen replay.

4.6 Deepfake Detection
The deepfake analyser uses three frequency-domain and geometric signals:
Corner frequency ratio — GAN checkerboard artefacts leave elevated energy at FFT corners relative to the centre
Chroma channel standard deviation — synthetic faces exhibit unnaturally uniform colour channels
Facial symmetry score — GAN models tend toward perfect bilateral symmetry unlike natural faces

The weighted composite produces a score from 0–100 and a letter grade (A–F). Scores below 50 are flagged as unsuitable for reliable recognition. This gate should be applied before embedding generation in production pipelines.

5.5 Voice Liveness — Active Challenge

Challenge
Active voice liveness asks the user to speak a randomised passphrase. The platform issues a text prompt and validates three properties of the returned audio:
Text-dependent verification — spoken words match the issued prompt (using a lightweight ASR confidence score)
Liveness signal — anti-spoof model scores the recording
Speaker match — embedding is compared against the enrolled voiceprint
All three checks must pass for the challenge to succeed. The session token expires after 60 seconds.

11.4 Responsible AI Considerations
Demographic estimation (gender/age) is provided as a technical feature for legitimate use cases such as age-verification gates and analytics. Deploying organisations are responsible for ensuring this feature is used in compliance with applicable anti-discrimination and privacy regulations. The platform does not infer race, religion, or political affiliation.
Liveness and deepfake detection reduce but do not eliminate the risk of sophisticated presentation attacks. High-security deployments should layer Aura's signals with additional verification factors (OTP, document check, human review) rather than relying on a single signal.
